To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) We design and evaluate a cooperative game - "GuessWhich" - to measure human-visual conversational agent performance; 2) We conduct a human study with 2 versions of ALICE and find that the version that outperforms the others when paired with an automated questioner bot performs worse when paired with humans, suggesting that there is a mismatch between how AI is evaluated in isolation vs. how AI is evaluated when paired with humans; 3) Our study also shows that
(1) We design a new cooperative game - Guess-Which - to measure the performance of human-visual-conversational-agent (human-AI) teams.

(1) the human-AI team is a better metric than AI in isolation, (2) the performance of human-ALICE does not correlate with the performance of AI-AI teams, and (3) human-AI performance can be improved by providing humans with a better interface to the AI.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: How can we evaluate the performance of visual conversational agents in the context of a human in the team?
the following questions: 1) how do we measure performance of human-AIs?
measuring the impact of AI on the performance of human teams and the design of human-AI cooperative games to this end.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the performance of a human-AI team is not just dependent on the performance of the AI, and is also dependent on the quality of the interaction between the human player and the AI agent.
the human-ALice team is more efficient than the human-ALicex team, but only when ALicex is not a good conversationalist.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we design a cooperative human-AI game to measure human-AV team performance and we find that performance of human-AV teams does not always translate from AI-AI performance.

we have designed a game for measuring human-AI team effectiveness and have used this game to demonstrate that the effectiveness of human-AI team can be impacted by the AI's performance, but also by the way in which the AI's performance is measured.
the performance of human-ALICE is not a monotonic function of the AI performance, i.e., there exists a non-monotonic relationship between human-AI performance and AI performance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need to benchmark AI not just in terms of its performance in isolation but also in the context of how it translates into performance of human-AIs teams.
it is crucial for AI to be evaluated in the context of its intended usage, and not in isolation.
we must design benchmarks that reflect real-world scenarios, and not just measure AI in isolation.
